Stocks, Gold, and Asia Bleed $2.2 Trillion: Top 5 Factors That Triggered the Crash. Photo by BeInCrypto

Global markets lost roughly $2.2 trillion on November 16 as US stocks, precious metals, and Asian equities sold off together. Technology and AI-linked names led the decline.

However, the rout did not stem from a single shock. Five key factors combined to unsettle investors.

The 5 Factors Behind the $2.2 Trillion Market Selloff

A market selloff is a rapid, broad decline in asset prices as investors rush to reduce risk. This time, the damage spread across several asset classes.

Market Bloodbath Wipes Out $2.2 Trillion. Source: X/@BullTheoryio

According to market data, the S&P 500 alone shed about $1.06 trillion. Separately, the Nasdaq lost $870 billion, the Dow $270 billion, and the Russell 2000 $55 billion.

Meanwhile, gold lost roughly $420 billion, silver $130 billion, and Asian stocks about $600 billion.

1. NVIDIA's Leadership Crisis

The main catalyst remained the fallout from Jensen Huang's abrupt resignation as NVIDIA CEO. Reports said the board was not considering his return.

Moreover, the board was reportedly weighing a national security investigation. His exit followed allegations involving a relationship that US authorities linked to Chinese intelligence interests.

As a result, chip stocks extended their losses. Investors also worried that disruption at NVIDIA could ripple across the entire AI ecosystem.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ewEUYZVu-gw

2. Fed Chair Warsh's Warning on AI Risks

Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh added to the unease. He outlined scenarios in which the AI investment boom fails to deliver expected returns.

In that case, Warsh noted, the economy could face falling stock valuations, slower growth, and higher unemployment. His remarks signaled that policymakers see real concentration risks in the AI trade.

3. Tighter Chip Export Restrictions

Semiconductor stocks also faced fresh policy pressure. The US tightened restrictions on overseas access to advanced chips, which deepened losses across the sector.

Intel fell more than 6% after a class action lawsuit alleged it misled investors about slowing PC sales. Meanwhile, Alphabet and Amazon each dropped about 3%.

As a result, the Nasdaq sank roughly 2.5%, while the VIX volatility index jumped nearly 24%.

4. Pre-Earnings Caution and Higher Yields

Investors also faced a busy calendar. NVIDIA reports earnings on Tuesday, while Anthropic's highly anticipated IPO arrives later this week.

At the same time, Treasury yields sit near multi-year highs, and the dollar keeps strengthening. Traders also expect further Fed rate hikes to fight sticky inflation.

That mix hurt growth stocks and non-yielding assets such as gold and silver. Meanwhile, Asian chip markets suffered steep overnight losses that spilled into US trading.

A 50% jump in Insulet (PODD) stock would depend on the people already using its Omnipod insulin pumps, a group management calls a substantial recurring revenue foundation. A rise that size is not new for this stock, since Insulet shares rose 50% or more from one close to a later close in the same year in eight of the last ten calendar years. Yet the stock fell 54.7% over the twelve months to November 13, 2026, while the S&P 500 returned 11.7%. Insulet's chance of another jump that size turns on those existing users. So how fast is the number of people using Omnipod still growing?

Insulet's Customer Base Grew More Than 20%

Management said on its November 4, 2026 call that Insulet's global customer base grew more than 20% from a year earlier in fiscal Q3 2026. New sign-ups grew far more slowly. During the quarter, new customer starts rose only in the low single digits. In the U.S., the customer base grew in the high teens, but new starts were flat.

The financial results reflected the larger customer base. Revenue rose 19.2% to $842 million in the quarter. Management said that the bigger customer base and stable pricing supported that growth. Outside the U.S., Omnipod revenue grew 31.7%, driven primarily by volume, management said.

The prescriber base is growing too. Nearly 34 thousand U.S. health care providers now prescribe Omnipod, up more than 20% year over year.

Slower 2027 Growth Meets A Ten-Year Low Multiple

On the same call, management said 2027 total company growth would come in modestly below the mid-teens framework it gave on its Q2 call, as it takes a more conservative approach, faces a tougher comparison and expects less price mix benefit abroad. Management also expects international growth to moderate meaningfully in 2027.

By the end of September, Insulet's sales multiple had hit a ten-year low. The stock was priced at 2.8 times sales at September 30, 2026, marking the lowest of the 40 quarter-ends since fiscal Q4 2016. It has since moved up to 3.3 times sales as of November 13. On earnings, though, the stock is not cheap. It trades at 24.7 times trailing profit, against 21.9 for the S&P 500.

Management still expects Insulet to deliver top tier growth on a multi-billion dollar revenue base in 2027 and to further expand profitability. The company is also buying back stock. It plans to spend $400 million on repurchases in the fourth quarter, funded with cash on hand. That spending is equal to about 3.8% of its market value on November 13.

IREN (NASDAQ:IREN), a vertically-integrated AI cloud and data center operator, closed at $16.39, down 9.80%. The neocloud provider extended its slide to a fresh 52-week low as AI infrastructure weakness and broader technology selling dominated trading. Investors are concerned about the future of the AI industry as they await semiconductor chip leader Nvidia's key quarterly earnings report, due Tuesday, to get a read on how the sector is faring.

Trading volume reached 78.8 million shares, coming in about 53% above its three-month average of 51.6 million shares. IREN IPO'd in 2021 and has fallen 33% since going public.

How the markets moved today

The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX:^GSPC) closed at 7,416, down 1.92%, while the Nasdaq Composite (NASDAQINDEX:^IXIC) closed at 24,510, down 2.49%. In data center infrastructure and AI cloud hosting stocks, sector rivals also slipped, with TeraWulf (NASDAQ:WULF) closing at $11.88, down 5.86%, and Cipher Digital (NASDAQ:CIFR) closing at $6.54, down 4.66%.

What this means for investors

On Monday, Nov. 16, IREN shares fell due to a broad tech sector sell-off, which added to Wall Street's wave of neocloud selling amid concerns for the future of the AI industry in the aftermath of Nvidia's former CEO Jensen Huang's resignation. Huang's involvement with a Nvidia customer contributed to exposing how Chinese businesses were illegally gaining access to AI semiconductor chips.

As a result, on Nov. 15, the U.S. government announced tighter controls over AI technology access. This contributed to Wall Street concerns over how the new regulations could impact the AI industry.

IREN stock was already under pressure because the company has about a $6 billion funding gap to achieve its fiscal 2027 infrastructure plan despite the artificial intelligence boom. Management noted that capital markets have become more selective, raising fears of potential shareholder dilution or higher borrowing costs.

Those fears were amplified on Monday when the benchmark 10-year Treasury yield rose past 5%, renewing debate over whether high AI capital expenditures would eventually pay off, weighing on high-growth tech stocks like IREN.

Today's biggest moves

Tyson Foods, Inc. shares surged 8.72% after the company exceeded quarterly earnings expectations and provided a positive outlook for its beef segment, but the broader market was weighed down by Nvidia Corporation, which fell 4.12% amid a leadership crisis. Elsewhere, Intel Corporation dropped 7.02% during a volatile session for semiconductors, and Dell Technologies Inc. slid 6.96% following warnings about industrywide debt.

What this means for investors

Today was a challenging day for tech stocks, with the Invesco QQQ Trust (NASDAQ:QQQ) falling 2.66% to $661.84 per share. This drop occurred as negative sentiment hit the sector on multiple fronts.

Aside from the ongoing struggles with Nvidia's leadership crisis, AMD stock suffered due to new export restrictions on advanced AI chips to Southeast Asian countries. Consequently, the stock fell by 5.58% to $504.28 per share.

Moreover, Federal Reserve Governor Michelle Bowman turned hawkish on corporate debt levels. This is concerning to hyperscalers like Meta Platforms, which depend heavily on debt financing to fund their AI build-outs.

Furthermore, the tech sector faces further tests this week when Nvidia announces its earnings for the third quarter of fiscal 2027 on Tuesday after the bell. This is Nvidia's first earnings call without CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang, and the announcement could offer hints on the company's direction going forward.

Additionally, Anthropic's IPO is set for Thursday. The company is set to price its IPO on Wednesday night, and how it performs Thursday and industry sentiment could influence its performance.

Indeed, investors face an unusual amount of uncertainty, though it is possible Nvidia's earnings report and Anthropic's IPO could ease some of those doubts. Knowing that, watching and waiting may be an AI investor's best strategy for now.

detail:
What Has Changed In Caterpillar's Story?

Caterpillar (CAT) stock trades at 23.3 times earnings, against 21.9 for the S&P 500. Shareholders paying that premium need to know what they are buying, and the company's priorities have changed. Management emphasized its merchandising programs in 2025, saying they stimulated higher-than-expected sales to users in North America. The company emphasized something else on its October 29, 2026 call. So what does management talk up now?

Caterpillar Now Talks Up Data Center Demand

Management pointed to very strong demand for turbines and large reciprocating engines used in data center applications on the fiscal Q3 2026 call. The company said power generation sales to users grew 75% in the quarter on the back of that demand. Those engines and turbines come from Power & Energy, the company's largest business.

Management's emphasis was on selling machines in 2025. On the fiscal Q1 2025 call, the company said its merchandising programs were yielding results. Management credited those programs with stronger sales to users in North America on the fiscal Q2 2025 call. The programs mattered then: management reported sales and revenues down 1% from a year earlier on that same Q2 call.

Management still credited the programs on its August 4, 2026 call during an answer about rental fleet loading and Major Projects, the Cat dealer-owned rental venture in its construction business. On the October call, management credited Construction Industries growth to retail sales and rental fleet loading.

How Big Are Caterpillar's Two Largest Businesses?

Power & Energy is the largest of Caterpillar's three primary segments: it brought in $32.2 billion in fiscal 2025, 47.6% of company revenue. Construction Industries brought in $25.1 billion, or 37.1%. Over that year the two moved apart, as Power & Energy revenue grew 11.6% while Construction Industries revenue slipped 1.6%.

That growth gap closed in fiscal Q3 2026. Power & Energy sales rose 18% to $8.8 billion, management said. Construction Industries kept pace with sales up 18% to $8 billion. Its sales of equipment to end users grew 20%, marking the seventh quarter in a row of growth from a year earlier, even with the programs out of the spotlight.

What Caterpillar's Data Center Focus Means For Shareholders

The new emphasis reads as reassuring so far for a holder. Construction Industries is growing without management making the case for its sales programs, and management said strong orders across all three main businesses lifted the backlog to a record $78 billion.

title: Investors: If a Market Correction Is Coming, This 1 Move Will Make or Break Your Portfolio
detail:
Investors: If a Market Correction Is Coming, This 1 Move Will Make or Break Your Portfolio
Leo Sun, The Motley Fool
Mon, November 16, 2026 at 3:50 PM CST 5 min read
^GSPC
NVDA
Trade NVIDIA on Coinbase
Trading disclosure

It's been more than four years since the last bear market ended on Oct. 12, 2022. But the average bull market lasts roughly four to five years, suggesting the next downturn could be right around the corner. The Iran war, elevated interest rates and Treasury yields, and other macro headwinds could certainly trigger a market crash over the next 12 months. But when that happens, one move will either make or break your portfolio.

What should investors remember about market crashes?

The S&P 500 (SNPINDEX: ^GSPC) has generated an average annual total return of more than 10% since its inception in 1957. Yet during those seven decades, the S&P 500 experienced 12 bear markets -- and each of those downturns shook out plenty of nervous investors.

Missed AI's "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 16x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we're only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue »

Image source: Getty Images.

Peter Lynch, who led Fidelity's Magellan Fund to beat the S&P 500 for over a decade, famously said: "Everybody in the world is a long-term investor until the market goes down." Warren Buffett also once said that if investors buy a stock, they need to be prepared for it to "go down 50% -- or more -- and be comfortable with it." But it's easier to recite those mantras than to follow them.

The key metrics to watch during a market crash

Many of the market's biggest crashes occurred after periods of "irrational exuberance". That term, coined by former Fed chairman Alan Greenspan in 1996, was originally a warning about rising stock market valuations during the dot-com boom.

At the peak of the dot-com bubble in March 2000, the S&P 500's trailing price-to-earnings ratio exceeded 30 as its forward P/E ratio exceeded 60. It subsequently experienced a peak-to-trough decline of nearly 50% before bottoming out in Oct. 2022. When it finally reached its nadir, it was trading at about 14 times and 29 times its trailing and forward P/E ratios, respectively.

Over the past several decades, the S&P 500 has traded an average trailing P/E ratio of 18-19 and a forward P/E ratio of about 17. As of this writing, the S&P 500 trades at 26 times trailing earnings and 18 times forward earnings. So while the S&P 500 looks historically expensive, it hasn't quite reached dot-com bubble levels yet.

If the market crashes, investors should watch the S&P 500's trailing multiple. If it sinks to the low teens, it makes more sense to hold on -- or buy more stocks -- and wait for a rebound. Doing so would be the one move that could either make or break your portfolio.
